title: Why Are Killer Whales Still Bumping Boats? A New Sinking Off Spain
summary:
Picture this: you're sailing on a sunny day off the coast of Spain, when suddenly a group of black-and-white killer whales starts ramming your boat's rudder. That's exactly what happened to two people on a 46-foot yacht last week. The orcas destroyed the rudder, and the sailors had to call for help. A coastguard boat towed them to safety.

This wasn't the only close call. Earlier that same week, another boat called the Idem sank after orcas broke its rudder. Luckily, both people on board were rescued. Since 2020, there have been over 700 reports of orcas interacting with boats — from gentle nudges to hours-long attacks. At least eight boats have been lost.

So why are these clever ocean mammals doing this? Some people online say it's revenge — that a female orca named White Gladis was hurt by a boat and now she's teaching others to fight back. But most scientists don't agree. They think it's more like a trend. Orcas are super social, and young ones learn by watching adults. It's like when a cool new dance move spreads through your school. The young orcas see the adults ramming rudders and think, "Hey, that looks fun!" Then they try it themselves.

Researchers have identified about 15 orcas involved, out of a tiny group of fewer than 50. This group is critically endangered because they depend on bluefin tuna for food. To stay safe, sailors are told to cut the engine, drop the sails, and let go of the wheel — giving the orcas nothing to push against. Boats that follow this advice usually get less damage. Scientists hope that by studying every encounter, they can solve this mystery and protect both people and these amazing animals.
why_it_matters: This shows that animal groups can develop new behaviors, just like trends among kids, and understanding them helps keep both people and wildlife safe.

background_read: Killer whales, or orcas, are actually the largest members of the dolphin family and live in every ocean.
The orcas involved in these boat encounters belong to a small population that lives near the Strait of Gibraltar (the narrow strip of water between Spain and Africa).
Since 2020, scientists have recorded hundreds of these interactions, and they are trying to understand why this unusual behavior started.
Article_Structure: WHO: A group of about 15 endangered killer whales (orcas) from a small population of fewer than 50.
WHAT: They have been ramming and breaking the rudders of boats, sinking at least eight vessels.
WHERE: In the waters off the coast of Spain, near the Strait of Gibraltar.
WHY: Scientists think young orcas are copying the adults, like a new fad, not because they want revenge.

perspectives.description: They feel unsafe and worried about damage to their boats, and want the behavior to stop.
They find this behavior fascinating because it shows how orcas learn from each other, and they hope to protect both animals and people.
They love seeing such smart animals, but they also want the orcas to stay safe and not be harmed by frightened sailors.
